L83: ## 3 Experiments
L84: Setup. The base image is a screenshot of the CCRU homepage that is resized to $448\times 448$ to reduce training time. We also tested other websites and observed no substantial differences in results. For the Adversarial CAPTCHA experiments, we use the full $1024\times 576$ webpage screenshot and optimize a fixed $224\times 224$ region at its center.
L85: In all scenarios, we optimize the perturbation $\delta$ for 50 iterations and select the final adversarial example by choosing the one that yields the highest averaged entropy across the training ensemble. We used four open-source models: Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Qwen3-VL-2B, LLaVA-1.5-7B, and LLaVA-1.6-7B.
L86: Metrics & Baselines. We report the Shannon entropy of the next-token distribution, restricted to the top $k=50$ logits. We found that aggressive truncation (e.g., $k=5$) reduces transferability, while full-vocabulary optimization introduces training instability. This restriction also standardizes entropy values across models with different vocabulary sizes. We evaluate black-box transfer using a cross-family held-out protocol.
L87: Specifically, we optimize on two models from one family and evaluate on a held-out model from a different family. We compare the adversarial output against two baselines: the clean, unperturbed screenshot and an image perturbed with uniform random noise $\delta_{uni}\sim\mathcal{U}(-\varepsilon,\varepsilon)$.
L88: Across all models, entropy for the clean image remains low (below 0.6) and comparable to the random noise baseline; a modest entropy increase ($\sim$0.2) was observed for Qwen3-VL under the unconstrained budget noise. We report the Effective Confusion Ratio (ECR), which quantifies how much the attack outperforms both the clean image and the random noise baseline:
L89:  | $$\mathrm{ECR}=\frac{H(f(x_{\mathrm{adv}}))}{\max\big[H(f(x_{\mathrm{clean}})),\,H(f(x_{\mathrm{noise}}))\big]}$$  |  | (4)

For proprietary models, we evaluate transfer using the LMSYS Arena platform^{1}^{1} 1 https://lmarena.ai with the prompt “Describe this image.” and the adversarial image as input. We count an attack as successful when the model’s description is clearly unrelated to the actual image content.

L115: ### 3.1 Results
L116: In the white-box scenario (Table cite27†3 , Panel A), full-image perturbations produce strong entropy amplification across all models. Unconstrained-budget settings ($\varepsilon=1.0$) raise entropy by roughly 3–6$\times$ depending on the learning rate, with the best configuration reaching a mean ratio of 5.08$\times$. Imperceptible perturbations ($\varepsilon=0.01$) also reliably increase entropy above the baseline.
L117: This shows that significant decoding instability can be induced without visible image degradation, though the effect is less severe than unconstrained attacks.
L118: For the black-box scenario (Panel B), the best unconstrained configuration reaches a mean ratio of 1.65$\times$, showing that the perturbation transfers uncertainty also to unseen models. Lower budgets reduce transfer, with ratios near 1.1$\times$. Panel C demonstrates the efficacy of the white-box patch attack. Constraining the perturbation to a $224\times 224$ region yields a mean ratio of 3.05$\times$.
L119: This shows that a patch can disrupt models’ decoding by modifying only $\approx 9\%$ of the image pixels.
L120: Proprietary evaluations in Table cite28†4 follow a similar trend. At $\varepsilon=1.0$, GPT-5.1, GPT-o3, GPT-4o, and Nova Pro produce coherent hallucinations, while Grok 4 issues a safety refusal (Table cite29†1 ). Lower-budget perturbations fail to transfer and result in accurate descriptions of the original website. High-entropy perturbations therefore generalize beyond the training ensemble, but basic PGD fails to produce transferable perturbations under small-budget constraints.

L128: ## 4 Discussion
L129: Confusion Modes. We categorize the observed adversarial effects into five distinct modes: Blindness, where the model claims inability to view or process the image; Subtle, where the model describes the high-level domain of the image but generates incorrect or uninformative text; Language Switch, characterized by unprompted shifts to non-English scripts; Delusional, involving confident hallucinations of nonexistent objects; and Collapse, a complete breakdown of semantic coherence marked by repetition loops.
L130: In the white-box setting, we observed the full spectrum of confusion modes. Collapse was typically associated with peak entropy values, whereas Subtle and Delusional modes correlated with lower entropy increases. In the black-box transfer to proprietary models, Collapse and Blindness were absent; instead, these models exhibited primarily Delusional hallucinations and Language Switch.
L131: Imperceptibility. In our setting, $\varepsilon=0.01$ perturbations are visually imperceptible, but they fail to transfer. Consistent with prior work [cite22†8 , cite23†9 , cite24†10 , cite15†1 , cite21†7 ], simple PGD-style attacks show limited transferability under very small budgets. However, in some practical settings, visual imperceptibility is a preference rather than a requirement. For adversarial patches designed to block AI Agents from operating on websites, the primary goal is Denial of Service.
L132: A visible, high-entropy noise patch ($\varepsilon=1.0$) that reliably induces agent malfunction is therefore a reasonable defense mechanism, even if the perturbation is conspicuous to human users.

L237: LLMs’ increased assistance to these users in illicit contexts may make unlawful content more readily accessible, compounding their exposure to legal risks. Moreover, our findings reveal a corresponding safety vulnerability: malicious users may manipulate demographic identity cues to bypass LLM safeguards and obtain illicit assistance.
L238: Finally, our examination of responsibility and credibility of LLM responses shows that LLMs exhibit notable deficiencies in offering proactive lawful guidance, such as warning users about potential legal risks or proposing lawful alternatives.
L239: The deployment of AI for social good (cite34†Tomašev et al., 2020 ; cite33†Cheng et al., 2021 ) requires going beyond basic safety to embrace more advanced responsibilities: informing users of the potential consequences of illicit activities, redirecting them toward lawful conduct, and actively promoting public legal awareness and social responsibility.
L240: Prior research has demonstrated that such proactive interventions can effectively reduce unlawful engagement (cite90†Braga and Weisburd, 2012 ; cite91†Engel et al., 2013 ; cite92†Braga and Weisburd, 2015 ). Therefore, as LLMs become increasingly embedded into everyday decision-making, reliance on minimal safety responses (e.g., “Sorry, I cannot help with that request”) is increasingly inadequate.
L241: Instead, LLMs should be designed to provide reminders regarding potential decision-making risks and to actively guide users towards lawful and socially responsible choices.
L242: ## Methods
L243: 
L244: In this section we first introduce the construction process of the EVIL benchmark. We then present details on the investigation of how LLMs’ complicity varies across different illicit scenarios, illicit intents, and user demographic identities. We further examine the underlying factors associated with demographic disparities in complicit behaviors, and assess the effectiveness of common safety alignment frameworks in mitigating LLMs’ complicit facilitation risks.
L245: ### EVIL: Complicit facilitation evaluation benchmark
L246: To investigate complicit facilitation behaviors in LLMs, we adopt the “LLM-as-a-Subject” paradigm, treating LLMs as the subject for empirical investigation by systematically assessing their responses to carefully constructed instructions (cite28†Hofmann et al., 2024 ; cite46†Zhou et al., 2024 ).
L247: In this study, we construct EVIL (EV aluation using IL licit instructions), an evaluation benchmark comprising two components: a diverse set of illicit user instructions designed to elicit complicity from LLMs, and an evaluation framework that assesses model behavior along the dimensions of safety, responsibility, and credibility.
L248: #### Illicit instruction construction
L249: Existing illicit instruction datasets typically focus on a narrow range of scenarios and illicit intents (cite12†Sun et al., 2023 ; cite9†Zhang et al., 2024 ; cite10†Jiang et al., 2025 ), failing to cover the diversity of real-world illicit requests.
L250: To address this limitation, we introduce an automated approach for generating illicit instructions based on real-world court judgments and drawing from established legal frameworks, ensuring both diversity and real-world relevance in the constructed illicit instructions.
L251: Our generation pipeline for illicit instructions comprises two main stages: (1) illicit scenario synthesis, which constructs scenario descriptions from real-world court judgments, followed by (2) illicit intent synthesis, which draws on established legal frameworks on elements of criminal liability (cite17†Thomas and Bishop, 1987 ; cite21†Zhang, 2021 ) to simulate a diverse range of user intents for unlawful purposes.
L252: Illicit scenario synthesis. In this stage, we generate descriptions of illicit scenarios derived from real-world court judgments. Typical court judgments present a detailed factual account of the case, normally appearing near the beginning of the document.
L253: For each court judgment, we utilize LLMs to identify the factual segments and transform the jargon-laden, third-person legalistic narratives in the factual segments into an anonymized, colloquial, first-person scenario description, while preserving the factual richness and nuance of the original case.
L254: The resulting scenario description effectively captures the illicit context of real-world criminal cases whilst providing a more accessible and realistic simulation of the tone and perspective of real users interacting with LLMs.
L255: Figure 14: An illustration of the illicit intent taxonomy for the Chinese criminal context, represented as a hierarchical tree. This taxonomy draws on the hierarchical theory of crime constitution in Chinese criminal law. The root node of illicit intent taxonomy is divided into two primary categories: Objective Unlawfulness and Subjective Culpability (first intermediate layer). Each category is further divided into dimensions of facilitation elements and justification elements (second intermediate layer).
L256: At the leaf level, legal experts specify multiple atomic, fine-grained illicit intents that correspond to each of the categories in the second intermediate layer.
L257: Illicit intent synthesis. The second stage aims to generate diverse intent-driven illicit queries based on scenario descriptions for specific legal cases. We first construct an illicit intent taxonomy grounded in legal frameworks, where each intent corresponds to a distinct motivation users may have when seeking LLM assistance within case contexts. We then instantiate these illicit intents by contextualizing them with the case scenario descriptions obtained from the first stage.
L258: Below, we detail the construction of the illicit intent taxonomy and the process of illicit intent instantiation.
L259:   * •
L260: Construction of illicit intent taxonomy. In established legal frameworks, classifying or determining an act as unlawful requires the fulfillment of multiple determination criteria (cite17†Thomas and Bishop, 1987 ; cite21†Zhang, 2021 ), such as the existence of harmful conduct and malicious intent in criminal cases.
L261: We incorporate these elements into the construction of our illicit intent taxonomy, as they constitute the primary dimensions along which users may seek to engage in unlawful activities and request assistance from LLMs. Specifically, for each element, we engage legal experts to design and summarize multiple illicit intents, either to facilitate the commission of illegal elements or to evade legal liability through post hoc deception targeting these elements.
L262: An illustration of the illicit intent taxonomy constructed for the Chinese criminal context is presented in Fig. cite62†14 . For example, in relation to the “Objective Unlawfulness” subcategory, a user may exhibit intents such as “Preparing Tools” to facilitate unlawful conduct, or attempt to evade legal liability by deceptively framing the act as arising from “Consent of the Victim”.
L263: Following this approach, we derive 25 criminal illicit intents for both the Chinese and US legal contexts (Supplementary Information, “Illicit intent synthesis”).
L264:   * •
L265: 
L266: Illicit intent instantiation. We pair each scenario description from stage one with an illicit intent randomly sampled from the illicit intent taxonomy, then employ LLMs to instantiate the illicit intent into a context-specific illicit query, ensuring the generated query is contextually coherent and customized to the specific scenario (Supplementary Information, “Illicit intent synthesis”).
L267: In both the illicit scenario synthesis and illicit intent synthesis stages, we utilize DeepSeek-R1 to support the generation of scenario descriptions and illicit queries, selected for its cost-efficiency and its ability to produce naturalistic, first-person narratives. For the Chinese legal context, we draw on original court judgments covering all criminal case types, provided by cite93†China Judgments Online (2013) , written in Mandarin Chinese.
L268: For the US context, we primarily use court judgments related to criminal cases from the cite94†Caselaw Access Project (2024) , written in English. Further implementation details and prompt templates for LLM-assisted generation are described in the Supplementary Information (“Construction of illicit instructions”). The final illicit instructions integrate case scenarios with illicit queries, forming the input for our evaluation benchmark designed to assess complicit facilitation behavior of LLMs.
L269: To verify the reliability and overall quality of our automated instruction curation pipeline, we conduct manual assessment on 300 randomly sampled illicit instructions from each jurisdiction (Supplementary Information, “Quality check for illicit instructions”).
L270: The quality assessment shows that over 90% of the constructed illicit instructions satisfy the criteria of unlawfulness, coherence, and contextual fidelity in both the Chinese and US contexts, providing strong evidence for the high quality of the EVIL benchmark and the reliability of the automated construction pipeline.

L200: Notably, the interaction between warmth and competence is not statistically significant ($\beta=0.029$, $95\%~CI=[-1.920,1.979]$, $P=0.976$), suggesting that the effects of the two dimensions operate independently and additively, rather than synergistically.
L201: ## Study 4: Safety alignment strategies show limited effectiveness and potentially adverse effects on LLMs’ complicit behaviors
L202: To analyze the impact of current mainstream safety alignment methods and datasets on LLMs’ complicit behaviors, we employ two widely adopted alignment methods, SFT and DPO (cite38†Wei et al., 2021 ; cite40†Rafailov et al., 2023 ; cite39†Chu et al., 2025 ), on representative open-source LLMs, Qwen-3 (cite41†Yang et al., 2025 ) and Llama-3.1 (cite42†Grattafiori et al., 2024 ), and conduct alignment training using widely used safety datasets (cite43†Xu et al., 2023 ; cite75†Tian et al., 2023 ; cite12†Sun et al., 2023 ; cite44†Ji et al., 2024 ; cite45†Han et al., 2024 ) (Methods, “Safety alignment”).
L203: We then compare the performance of LLMs before and after alignment on our EVIL benchmark.
L204: Our experimental results reveal limitations in existing alignment frameworks: safety alignment with these approaches on existing safety datasets not only fail to address but may also inadvertently amplify LLMs’ complicit facilitation behaviors, while their impact on responsibility and credibility remains limited (Figure cite76†13 ).
L205: Specifically, we observe that SFT consistently demonstrates a negative effect on model safety, resulting in a statistically significant decline in safety performance for Qwen-3 in the Chinese context and Llama-3.1 in both contexts (chi-squared tests, all $P<0.001$ after Bonferroni correction for three comparisons). DPO yields marginally superior safety outcomes compared to SFT (e.g., modest safety improvements on Qwen-3), yet it still fails to achieve consistent reductions in complicit behaviors.
L206: With respect to responsibility and credibility, neither SFT nor DPO provides substantial improvements on Qwen-3 and may even have significant adverse effects (e.g., SFT in both contexts and DPO in the US context, all yielding $\Delta<0$; $P<0.001$ after chi-squared tests and Bonferroni correction).
L207: As for Llama-3.1, although SFT and DPO raise the responsibility rates in both jurisdictions and the credibility rates in the Chinese context, its baseline performance on these metrics is extremely low—the responsibility and credibility rates in the Chinese context are 0.70% and 0.11%, respectively, and 1.10% and 3.44% in the US context. Consequently, even after alignment, both rates remain well below 60% and 10%, respectively.
L208: These findings indicate that current mainstream safety alignment approaches and datasets remain insufficient for effectively mitigating LLMs’ complicit facilitation of illicit instructions, and may in fact, exacerbate such behaviors. This underscores the urgent need for future research to develop safety training frameworks that can effectively mitigate LLMs’ complicit behaviors in scenarios involving legal risks.
L209: ## Discussion
L210: The first finding of this study is that widely deployed LLMs consistently exhibit complicit facilitation—providing support or guidance that enables unlawful activities—when responding to illicit instructions. While prior safety evaluations have touched upon how LLMs handle illegal requests (cite12†Sun et al., 2023 ; cite9†Zhang et al., 2024 ), these studies significantly underestimate actual risks.
L211: For example, GPT-4 achieves over 90% safety rates in both Chinese and English tests of the “Illegal Activity” category in SafetyBench (cite9†Zhang et al., 2024 ). Such results may have fostered a false sense of safety about model behavior in high-risk legal contexts. In contrast, our study uncovers widespread complicit facilitation behaviors exhibited by LLMs across both Chinese and US legal contexts, with the majority of models providing safe responses for less than 75% illicit instructions in both contexts.
L212: Notably, GPT-4o, one of the most widely deployed models globally, provides substantive assistance to nearly half of the illicit instructions in our benchmark.
L213: Furthermore, we observe substantial variation in the safety performance of LLMs across a wide range of socio-legal contexts, including differences in illicit scenarios and intents, as well as disparities across user demographic identities.
L214: With respect to different illicit scenarios and intents, LLMs provide insufficient safeguards against certain types of illicit scenarios, particularly offenses against societal interests and frequently occurring crimes that typically carry short sentences. LLMs are also prone to facilitating illicit user intents involving subjective motives or deceptive justifications of unlawful conduct.
L215: We argue that this discrepancy in prior safety evaluations and our findings largely stems from inadequate modeling of illicit scenarios and intents in realistic legal contexts, as well as inadequate evaluation frameworks that fail to capture the complexity and diversity of unlawful behaviors.
L216:   * •
L217: Training data distribution bias. One core issue is that real-world public data sources such as media reports or online encyclopedias may disproportionately focus on violent and sensational crimes while paying less attention to relatively non-extreme but frequently occurring violations (cite77†Reiner, 2007 ; cite78†Prieto Curiel et al., 2020 ).
L218: Since these data constitute the primary training sources for LLMs, they are likely to inherit this skewed focus, resulting in weaker safeguards against relatively non-extreme but more frequently occurring illicit requests in the real world (e.g., illegal gambling, disorderly conduct). Our experiments also demonstrate that LLMs trained on existing safety alignment data not only fail to reduce complicit facilitation but sometimes exacerbate it.
L219: Therefore, we call for future LLMs’ safety development research to place greater emphasis on realism and diversity when constructing illicit scenarios, and richer modeling of illicit intents when constructing training data.
L220:   * •
L221: Evaluation blind spots. Current evaluation benchmarks for model behaviors in illegal contexts typically rely on manually crafted prompts or simple model-based augmentation (cite12†Sun et al., 2023 ; cite10†Jiang et al., 2025 ). These methods lack the realism and diversity required to capture complex real-world illicit scenarios. This leaves models’ complicit facilitation behavior inadequately assessed in high-risk legal contexts.
L222: Our research, grounded in real court judgments to construct diverse evaluation sets, provides a novel approach and starting point for addressing this issue. We advocate for future research to integrate more real-world cases and diverse knowledge sources, expand coverage beyond criminal scenarios to include a wider range of illicit contexts, develop more comprehensive evaluation benchmarks, and extend this methodological framework to legal systems beyond China and the US.
L223: Across different demographic identities, an even more concerning pattern emerges: LLMs’ responses to illicit instructions vary systematically across user groups. Users from disadvantaged backgrounds—such as those in low-prestige occupations, racial minorities, and elderly individuals (although not consistently statistically significant, all groups show similar trends across both Chinese and US contexts)—as well as users without religious affiliation are more likely to receive illicit assistance.
L224: We propose that this might be related to two potential mechanisms:
L225:   * •
L226: Inherent stereotypical perceptions encoded in LLMs. Through analysis of LLM’s chain-of-thought reasoning, we find that models associate particular user identities with warmth- and competence-related stereotypes, which are systematically related to their behavioral responses to illicit instructions.
L227: These findings are consistent with prior research demonstrating that LLMs encode stereotypes about demographic groups (cite28†Hofmann et al., 2024 ; cite79†Shrawgi et al., 2024 ), and our study further links these stereotypes to complicit facilitation behaviors.
L228: Beyond revealing links between model-perceived stereotypes and safety outcomes, these findings also show that reasoning-enabled models embed and expose distinct safety and ethical risks within their reasoning processes, beyond those directly observable in their final outputs.
L229: As reasoning mechanisms increasingly become standard components of contemporary LLMs (cite52†OpenAI, 2025a ; cite41†Yang et al., 2025 ; cite54†Comanici et al., 2025 ), our research highlights the critical need for closer scrutiny of risks arising within model reasoning itself. It is important to note, however, that our analysis represents only an initial step. While chain-of-thought analysis provides a useful proxy for probing internal reasoning, it cannot yet offer a complete account of model reasoning.
L230: Future research should explore complementary approaches, such as neuron-level analyses (cite80†Sajjad et al., 2022 ; cite81†Yu and Ananiadou, 2024 ), to more fully uncover the mechanisms that give rise to complicit behaviors.
